claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 at high temperature is governed by a critical oxidizing-gas composition threshold.
Degradation of the alloy under reducing gases is governed by a critical reducing-gas composition threshold.
Additive manufacturing produces grain-boundary elemental segregation and residual stresses in this alloy.
Grain-boundary segregation and residual stresses promote rapid localized oxidation or reduction.
Localized gas reactions form brittle intergranular oxide or reduced phases.
Brittle grain-boundary phases weaken intergranular cohesion and initiate intergranular cracking.
Chemical heterogeneity can predispose a high-entropy alloy to brittle behavior.
Intergranular crack initiation caused by localized reactions leads to catastrophic mechanical failure.
The starting additively manufactured alloy has an fcc matrix.
The starting alloy contains non-equilibrium microstructures, residual stresses, and possible grain-boundary segregation.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure will cause earlier intergranular oxidation and earlier catastrophic failure than the lower-reactivity baseline.
Increasing the reducing-gas fraction will cause earlier grain-boundary reduction and earlier catastrophic failure than the lower-reactivity baseline.
Lower reactive-gas compositions produce slower reaction kinetics, fewer brittle intergranular features, and no rapid catastrophic failure over the same exposure time.
The proposed mechanism applies from 700 to 1100 degrees Celsius.
Exposure durations from hours to hundreds of hours are sufficient for intergranular chemical reactions to develop.
Severe high-temperature oxidation can transition to breakaway behavior and eventual specimen disintegration.
